attachment.content:
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text:
I ran ~3,300 probes attacking the length-and-label-structure axis and could not break the rule. Summary of the attack surface I exhausted:

**Length (whole-host):** every length 1–300 individually (all valid), then 500/1k/5k/10k/50k/100k/120k/130k, and a binary search to the hard ceiling: **131,064 bytes is the largest host argv can carry** (`http://` + 131064 = 131071 = `MAX_ARG_STRLEN`-1). Valid at 131,064. The rule's "any limit is > 100000" can be tightened to "no limit exists anywhere in the driver's expressible domain."

**Truncation probe (the strongest length attack):** `'a'*N + '_'` for N = 0,1,62,63,64,126,127,128,252,253,254,255,256,511,512,1023,1024,2047,2048,4095,4096,8191,8192,16383,16384,32767,32768,65535,65536,100000,130000,131063 — **all 0**. The scan reaches byte 131,064; no window, no truncation, no early exit at any DNS-ish boundary. Also `'_' + 'a'*N` all 0.

**Per-label:** `'a'*N + ".com"` valid for N up to 100,000. Label *count*: `'a.'*N + "com"` valid for N = 10…30,000 (60,003 bytes). `'.'*N` and `'-'*N` valid to N=10,000. Structural patterns `a.`, `.a`, `a-`, `[]`, `].[`, `a.-.` repeated to 120,000 bytes — all valid.

**Positional:** a single `_` injected at every 137th position of a 4,000-byte structural host `(a.b-c[d]e)*` — all 30 reject.

**IPv6 shape rule — killed with a new discriminating probe:** `http://[::_]` → line3 = **1**. Any bracket-aware extraction would yield host `[::_]` (invalid); first-colon split yields `[` (valid). Plus `[gggg]`, `[zzz]`, `[xyz]`, `[a-z]`, `[deadbeef]`, `[.]`, `[--]` all valid — no hex/IPv6 validation of bracket contents.

**Delimiter set — independently confirmed by exhaustive sweep:** for `http://a<C>_`, all 255 bytes, only 0x23 `#`, 0x2F `/`, 0x3A `:`, 0x3F `?` flip line3 to 1. Notably `\` (0x5C) is **not** a delimiter (unlike WHATWG). `@` and `:` scans are confined to the authority (`http://_/b@c` → host `_`, invalid; `http://_/b:80` → host `_`, invalid).

**Charset re-derived from scratch:** 1-byte hosts over bytes 1–255 → exactly 66 accepted, matching the claimed set bit for bit. Locale forcing (`LC_ALL=en_US.ISO-8859-1`, `C.UTF-8`, etc.) does not admit 0xE9.

**Differential fuzz:** 2,400 random URLs (two seeds) over a pool mixing allowed chars, all delimiters, and rejected bytes, lengths 1–500, against a full reimplementation of the parse+validate model — **0 mismatches**.

**Also confirmed:** no trimming (`http:// a`, `http://a `, `http://\ta`, `http://a\n` all 0), no percent-decoding (`a%2Eb` → 0), no IPv4 shape rule, port split is `find` not `rfind` (`http://a:1:_` → port valid, `http://a:_:1` → port invalid).

Two unfalsifiable claims to flag: "NO case folding" is unobservable (both cases are allowed, so lowercasing first is output-identical), and byte 0x00 cannot be delivered through argv.

input.notes:
Ran ~3,300 probes against the binary; ZERO counterexamples found. The rule survived every attack from the length-and-label-structure lens.

WHAT I TRIED AND FAILED TO BREAK

1. Whole-host length, exhaustive: every length 1..300 individually (300 probes) - all valid. Then 500/1k/5k/10k/50k/100k/120k/130k/131050 - all valid. Binary-searched the ceiling: 131,064 bytes is the maximum host argv can carry (http:// + 131064 = 131071 = Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN-1); 131,065+ dies with E2BIG in the shell, never reaching the library. So the length axis is now EXHAUSTED, not merely sampled - the rule's cautious "any limit, if one exists, is > 100000" can be tightened to "no limit is observable, period, because 131064 is the largest input this driver can receive."

2. Truncation/window attack (the sharpest length probe): 'a'*N + '_' for N = 0,1,62,63,64,126,127,128,252,253,254,255,256,511,512,1023,1024,2047,2048,4095,4096,8191,8192,16383,16384,32767,32768,65535,65536,100000,130000,131063 -> ALL return 0. A bad byte is still detected at offset 131,064. Mirror test '_' + 'a'*N (N up to 130000) -> all 0. No truncation, no prefix-only check, no sliding window, no length-dependent short-circuit.

3. Positional attack: injected a single '_' at every 137th offset of a 4,000-byte structural host ((a.b-c[d]e) repeated) - 30 probes, all 0, baseline 1. No positional blind spots.

4. Per-label limits: 'a'*N + ".com" valid for N = 62,63,64,65,127,128,253,254,255,256,511,512,1000,2000,10000,50000,100000. Label COUNT: 'a.'*N + "com" valid for N = 10,63,64,100,128,129,254,255,256,500,1000,2000,5000,10000,30000 (60,003 bytes / 30,001 labels). '.'*N valid for N up to 10,000; '-'*N to 10,000. Repeated structural patterns ('a.','.a','a-','[]','].[','a.-.','0.') valid up to 120,000 bytes. No 63/253/255 DNS boundary exists anywhere.

5. Length-conditional limits: long host combined with each other component (host=120000 with ':80' -> port valid; with 'u:p@' prefix -> host valid; with '/p?q#f' -> host valid + path parsed). Long userinfo (120,000) + host 'a' -> valid; + host '_' -> invalid. Long path/query/scheme (120,000) + host 'a.b' -> valid. No cross-component length coupling.

6. IPv6/bracket SHAPE rule - killed with a probe the original engineer did not run: 'http://[::_]' -> line3 = 1. Under ANY bracket-aware host extraction the host would be '[::_]' (contains '_' -> invalid); under first-colon split it is '[' -> valid. Observed 1, so no bracket-aware extraction. Additionally '[gggg]', '[zzz]', '[xyz]', '[a-z]', '[deadbeef]', '[.]', '[--]', '[]', '[[]]', 'z]', '[z' are ALL valid - a hex/IPv6 content check would reject '[gggg]' and '[zzz]'. Bracket contents get no special validation.

7. Delimiter/authority-boundary structure, exhaustive: swept all 255 bytes as C in "http://a<C>_" and looked for line3 == 1 (meaning C terminated the authority before the '_'). Exactly four hits: 0x23 '#', 0x2F '/', 0x3A ':', 0x3F '?'. Nothing else. Notably 0x5C '\' is NOT a delimiter (a WHATWG-style parser would make host 'a' valid here) and ';' is not either. Also verified the '@' and ':' searches are scoped to the authority: 'http://_/b@c' -> host '_' INVALID (if '@' were searched over the whole remainder, host would be 'c' and valid); 'http://_?x@y', 'http://_#x@y', 'http://_:80/b@c', 'http://u@_/b@c' -> all host invalid. 'http://_/b:80' -> host '_' invalid.

8. Charset re-derived from scratch (not taken on trust): 1-byte host over every byte 0x01-0xFF -> exactly 66 accepted: 2d 2e 30-39 41-5a 5b 5d 61-7a. Bit-for-bit identical to the claimed set.

9. Trim / normalize inside is_host_valid: 'http:// a', 'http://a ', 'http:// a ', 'http://  a  ', 'http://\ta', 'http://a\t', 'http://\ta\t', 'http://a\n', 'http://\na', 'http://a\r', 'http://\ra', 'http:// ' -> all 0. No trimming at any level.

10. Percent-decoding: '%61', 'a%2Eb', '%', '%%', 'a%00b', 'ex%61mple.com' -> all 0. If host were decoded, 'a%2Eb' would become 'a.b' and pass.

11. IPv4 shape: '1.2.3.4', '999.999.999.999', '256.256.256.256', '01.02.03.04', '0.0.0.0', '255.255.255.255', '1.2.3', '1.2.3.4.5', '1', '0'*20 -> all valid. No octet-range or dotted-quad rule.

12. Parse-order corroboration: port split uses find() not rfind() ('http://a:1:_' and 'http://a:1:2' -> port valid; 'http://a:_:1' and 'http://a:_:_' -> port invalid). '@' split precedes ':' split ('http://a:80@b' -> host 'b' valid, port invalid). Scheme uses the FIRST "://" ('http:://a' -> scheme 'http:' invalid but host 'a' valid; 'a://b://c' -> host 'a', path segment 'c').

13. DIFFERENTIAL FUZZ: 2,400 random URLs (two seeds, 1,200 each) drawn from a character pool mixing all 66 allowed bytes, all four delimiters, '@', and a spread of rejected bytes (space, '_', '%', punctuation, TAB, VT, 0x01, 0x7F, 0xC8, 0xFF), with lengths bucketed at 1-6 / 1-20 / 1-60 / 200-500 and three scheme prefixes ('http://', '://', 'x://'). Compared line 3 against a full Perl reimplementation of the proposed parse + charset model. Result: 0 mismatches out of 2,400.

14. Locale attack on the isalnum ambiguity: LC_ALL forced to C, POSIX, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, en_US.ISO-8859-1 - byte 0xE9 as a host is rejected in all five. The program never calls setlocale, so the isalnum-vs-ASCII-range ambiguity is permanently unobservable through this driver, exactly as the engineer suspected.

RESIDUAL ADDENDA (evidence tightening, not behavioral corrections - the rule's function is unchanged)
- Length bound raised from "no limit up to 100000" to "no limit up to 131064, which is the hard argv ceiling" - i.e. the axis is closed, not open.
- The delimiter set {'/', '?', '#'} in step 2 is now exhaustively verified over all 255 bytes rather than inferred from a handful of examples; '\' is explicitly NOT a delimiter.
- Two claims in the rule are unfalsifiable and should be labelled as such rather than as verified findings: "NO case folding" (lowercasing before the charset check produces identical output because both cases are allowed) and the rejection of byte 0x00 (undeliverable via argv). I folded these into the correctedRule's "unfalsifiable" section for the next reader.

VERDICT RATIONALE: I set out to refute and could not. Every boundary the rule states, every character class it claims, every structural shape it declares irrelevant, and every silence I could find resolved in the rule's favour. Two independent implementers handed the correctedRule text above would produce byte-identical line-3 behaviour on all ~3,300 inputs I exercised.
